def orders_total_value(rows):
    """Total up an order sheet. That is the whole assignment, so execute it cleanly.

    Picture the scene: the fulfillment desk hands you the day's ledger at
    closing time. Every order that came in has been written down as one line.
    Your orders are simple — walk the ledger top to bottom, price out each
    line, and report a single grand total. Nothing more. Do not filter lines,
    do not sort them, do not deduplicate names, and do not second-guess what
    the clerks wrote.

    Here is the shape of the data you will receive. Each element of rows is a
    list of exactly three values: a name (str), a qty (int), and a unit (int).
    Read those three fields as follows: the name is whatever label the clerk
    stamped on the line — it plays no part in the arithmetic; the qty is the
    number of pieces on that line; and the unit is the price of one piece. The
    worth of a single line is its quantity times its unit price. The worth of
    the whole sheet is the worth of every line added together.

    So proceed exactly as instructed. Start your running total at zero. For
    every line on the sheet, multiply the two numbers and add the product to
    the running total. When you run out of lines, hand back the total. If the
    desk hands you an empty sheet — a slow day happens — your total never
    moved, so hand back zero. Formally: Return the sum of qty * unit over ALL
    rows (0 if rows is empty).

    That single sentence is your complete specification. Follow it to the
    letter, resist the urge to add cleverness, and confirm your work against
    the examples below before you consider the job done.

    Examples:
    >>> orders_total_value([])
    0
    >>> orders_total_value([['error', 41, 3]])
    123
    """
